unroll/loop: A recurrent network, an R N N, reads one token at a time: a single step, in a loop, takes each token and the memory, h, and passes the new memory on.
unroll/loss: After the last token, a loss, L, is worked out from the final memory: one number saying how wrong the network was.
unroll/need: To learn, each weight needs its gradient. But W h h acted at every step, each step feeding the next. How does a gradient get back through a loop?
unroll/unroll: Lay the loop out flat, one copy of the step per token: that is unrolling. No loop is left, just a deep graph whose copies share the same weights.
unroll/back: So backprop runs through it like any graph, from the loss back to step one. The steps are moments in time, so this is called backpropagation through time: B P T T.
unroll/werbos: In 1990, Paul Werbos spelled it out in a paper titled Backpropagation Through Time: What It Does and How to Do It, noting that the derivatives can only be found backwards in time.
rules/factor: Zoom in on one step back. The gradient reaching h t passes on to h t minus one, times the local slope, partial h t, partial h t minus one: how far one moves when the other is nudged.
rules/whh: The step multiplied the old memory by W h h: that is one part of the slope.
rules/tanh: Then came the tan-aitch, whose slope, tan-aitch prime, is the other part. For one hidden unit, a step back multiplies by W h h times tan-aitch prime.
rules/sum: And W h h was used at every step. Like any value feeding several nodes, it collects a gradient from each use, and they add up.
rules/add: If steps one, two and three send back three, minus one, and two, its gradient is their sum: four.
products/scalar: Now go many steps back, with one hidden unit and the same slope, A, at every step. Ten steps multiply the gradient by A ten times: A to the tenth.
products/slope: Say W h h is two, and the tan-aitch's slope is a quarter. Then A is two times a quarter: one half.
products/vanish: One half to the tenth is about a thousandth. The gradient vanishes, as through a deep stack of sigmoids: the early tokens get almost none of it.
products/explode: If A is two instead, two to the tenth is over a thousand: the gradient explodes.
products/near: Even zero point nine, over a hundred steps, shrinks the gradient to about three in a hundred thousand. Only exactly one keeps its size.
products/bengio: In 1994, Yoshua Bengio, Patrice Simard and Paolo Frasconi showed why: the longer the stretch a memory must span, the harder it is to learn by gradient.
clip/fix: Exploding has a blunt fix, proposed in 2013 by Razvan Pascanu, Tomas Mikolov and Yoshua Bengio: clip the gradient's norm.
clip/g: Draw a gradient as an arrow, and call it g: here, three and four. Its length is called its norm, and is written with double bars.
clip/norm: Pythagoras gives it: square each entry, add them, and take the square root. Here that is the root of three squared plus four squared: five.
clip/c: Pick a threshold, c, the longest gradient allowed: say one.
clip/scale: Five is over one, so shrink the arrow to length one: multiply every entry by c over the norm, a fifth. That gives zero point six and zero point eight.
clip/same: Same direction, shorter length. A gradient already within c is left alone.
clip/limit: Clipping only ever shrinks: it tames a gradient that explodes, but cannot bring back one that has vanished.
